quests.instruction: What is the most effective way to raise this?
quests.scene: Your table ordered forty minutes ago and the food still hasn't come. Your waiter walks past.
options: We've been waiting forty minutes for our food now — could you check with the kitchen?
We ordered a long time ago, and I'm starting to wonder whether the kitchen has forgotten about us entirely.
This is unacceptable service. I want to speak to the manager right now about the delay.
No rush at all, we're happy to wait as long as it takes today, though we do have a film to catch later this evening.
quests.hint: Give the fact and ask for a specific action.
quests.explanation: Stating the wait and asking him to check is clear and actionable. Hinting, escalating straight to a manager, or pretending it doesn't matter gets less useful results.
quests.culturalNote: Waiters usually respond well to a specific time and request; hints often get missed.

quests.instruction: Choose the clearest way to handle this.
quests.scene: You booked a sea-view room, but your room looks over the car park. You're at reception.
options: I paid extra for a sea view, so I expect you to fix this immediately, or I'll ask for a full refund.
This isn't the room I booked, but it's fine, I suppose, as long as the bed is comfortable and quiet.
I booked a sea-view room, and this looks over the car park. Could you tell me what options there are?
There seems to be a slight mix-up with the room, and I wonder if perhaps something could be done.
quests.hint: State the mismatch and ask what can be done.
quests.explanation: Naming the mismatch and asking for options invites a solution. Threats, giving in, or vague hints don't move things forward.
quests.culturalNote: Hotels often have some flexibility on room changes if asked early.

quests.scene: An online seller sent a phone with a cracked screen. You have photos and want it resolved quickly.
options: The item was damaged when it arrived. This is very disappointing, and I expect a full refund and an apology.
My order arrived damaged, but I'm sure it wasn't your fault. Could you possibly help me with it?
I received a damaged item. I've left a one-star review until this is resolved to my satisfaction.
My order arrived with a cracked screen (photo attached). I'd like either a replacement or a refund — which can you arrange fastest?
quests.hint: Include evidence and offer the seller a choice.
quests.explanation: Evidence plus two acceptable outcomes makes it easy to say yes quickly. Demands, over-softening, or review threats slow or sour things.
quests.culturalNote: Consumer rights differ by country, but photos and clear requests help in most cases.

quests.instruction: What is the most constructive way to raise this?
quests.scene: Your neighbor's dog barks every morning and you're losing sleep. You've never spoken to him about it.
options: Your dog barks every morning, and I'm getting tired of being woken up by it. Please do something.
I wanted to mention the barking in the mornings — it's been hard for me to sleep. Could we think of a solution together?
I don't want to cause trouble, but your dog has been a little loud recently, if you've noticed.
If your dog keeps barking, I'll have to report it to the council, and I'd rather avoid that.
quests.hint: Explain the effect on you and invite a joint fix.
quests.explanation: Describing the impact and inviting cooperation avoids blame. Demands, hints, or threats make him defensive or miss the point.
quests.culturalNote: A friendly first conversation usually works better than a formal complaint.

quests.instruction: Which response is the most constructive?
quests.scene: Your labelled lunch has gone missing from the office fridge for the second time.
options: Hey, I think someone took my labelled lunch from the fridge again — did you happen to see anything?
Someone keeps eating my lunch. Whoever it is, please stop, because it isn't funny and it isn't fair.
It's not a big deal, but my lunch went missing again this week, and I wanted to let everyone in the office know about it.
I'll start locking my lunch in my drawer, since clearly some people here can't be trusted.
quests.hint: Ask a neutral question instead of accusing anyone.
quests.explanation: A neutral, specific question gets information without blame. General accusations or sarcastic remarks poison the atmosphere.
quests.culturalNote: Office fridge disputes are common and best handled without singling anyone out.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to raise this.
quests.scene: Your roommate has been eating your food. You'd like to solve it without a fight.
options: You keep eating my food without asking, and I'm fed up with having to hide everything.
It's fine to borrow things sometimes, but perhaps it would be nice to ask first, if that's okay.
I'm going to buy a lock for the fridge, since you clearly can't respect my things.
I've noticed my food's going missing. Can we agree on what's shared and what isn't?
quests.hint: State the observation and propose a rule.
quests.explanation: Describing what you've noticed and proposing shared rules invites agreement. Complaints, mixed messages, or ultimatums don't.
quests.culturalNote: Shared-living agreements work best when set up as mutual rules.

quests.instruction: Which response would reduce the tension?
quests.scene: A customer is shouting at you at a service desk about a delayed order.
options: I can hear how frustrating this is, and I want to sort it out. Let me look at your order right now.
Please calm down, sir, and lower your voice, because shouting won't help me to solve your problem.
I'm sorry you feel that way, but I'm afraid that's our policy, and there's nothing I can change.
I understand you're upset, but I'll need you to stop raising your voice or I'll have to call security.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the feeling, then act.
quests.explanation: Naming the frustration and immediately acting lowers heat. Telling someone to calm down, policy shields, or threats escalate.
quests.culturalNote: 'Calm down' tends to increase anger in English-speaking service contexts.

quests.scene: Two colleagues begin arguing in a meeting you're leading.
options: You're both being unprofessional, and this argument is wasting everyone's time, so please stop now.
Let's pause — can we hear each point one at a time?
Maybe we should take a short break and come back to this discussion later, once everyone has had a chance to calm down.
I think you're both making valid points, so let's just move on to the next item on the list.
quests.hint: Bring structure to the disagreement.
quests.explanation: Offering a simple structure lets both be heard. Scolding, postponing, or skipping don't resolve the issue.
quests.culturalNote: Turn-taking is a familiar technique for facilitating heated discussions.

quests.scene: A friend snaps, 'You never listen to me!' You do listen, but she feels unheard.
options: That's not true, and you know it, because I listened to you for two hours last week.
I'm sorry you feel like I never listen, but I do try my best when we talk.
Maybe you should tell me things more clearly, so I don't have to guess what's going on.
I don't want you to feel unheard. Tell me what I missed, and I'll listen properly.
quests.hint: Address the feeling and invite her to explain.
quests.explanation: Focusing on her experience and asking for detail opens the conversation. Defending, conditional apologies, or blame shut it down.
quests.culturalNote: 'I'm sorry you feel' is often heard as defensive; naming her experience works better.

quests.scene: A colleague asks if you took his stapler. You didn't, and you're a little offended.
options: I didn't take your stapler, and I find it insulting that you would think I did.
Why would I take a stapler? Check your own desk first, before you start accusing people.
I don't know where it is, but I'm sure it will turn up somewhere around the office at some point, so don't worry too much.
I haven't seen your stapler, but I'll help you have a look around the desk.
quests.hint: Answer the question and keep the mood light.
quests.explanation: A short, honest answer plus an offer to help avoids escalation. Taking offense or shrugging it off makes it bigger or dismissive.
quests.culturalNote: Small accusations are best defused without defensiveness.

quests.scene: Your manager says you've been late several times. Two of the dates are true, but one was a cancelled train.
options: I'm not always late, and the trains are unreliable, so I don't think it's fair to blame me.
You're right, I'm a disaster, and I'll do better, and I'm so sorry about all of it.
I was late on Tuesday and Thursday, and I take that seriously. Last Monday was a train cancellation, though.
Everyone's late sometimes, so it seems unfair to pick on me when others do the same.
quests.hint: Own what's true and clarify what isn't.
quests.explanation: Accepting your part and correcting the one unfair date is honest and credible. Denial, over-apology, or comparisons don't help.
quests.culturalNote: Distinguishing between fair and unfair points shows maturity.

quests.scene: Your teacher says you were talking during a test. It was actually someone behind you.
options: It wasn't me, it was Jordan, so please don't put the blame on me for what someone else did.
I'm sorry, it won't happen again, and I'll try to be quieter for the rest of the class.
I wasn't talking, but I know it was noisy back there. Would it help if I moved to the front?
That's really unfair, and I think you should have checked before accusing me in front of everybody.
quests.hint: Deny calmly and offer a solution without blaming.
quests.explanation: Stating the facts and offering a fix avoids naming classmates. Blaming, false apology, or angry protest weaken your case.
quests.culturalNote: Naming other students rarely helps and can create new conflict.

quests.instruction: Choose the best response to the dispute.
quests.scene: Your landlord is withholding part of your deposit for 'damage' that you think is normal wear and tear.
options: I'd like to go through the deductions together. Could you send an itemized list with photos?
You can't keep my deposit for normal wear and tear, and I'll go to a tenants' union if you try.
I suppose I could pay for the carpet, if that's what you think is fair for both of us.
I'd rather not argue about this, so just keep whatever you think is right, that's fine.
quests.hint: Ask for evidence before agreeing or arguing.
quests.explanation: Asking for itemization and photos is firm and fair. Threats, giving in, or walking away skip the evidence.
quests.culturalNote: Deposit rules vary by country, so checking local tenant guidance is wise.

quests.instruction: What is the best way to propose a solution?
quests.scene: You and a coworker both want the desk by the window.
options: I've had this desk longer than you, so I think it's only fair that I keep it for good.
I'm happy to move to a different desk if it makes you more comfortable, so just let me know which one you'd prefer.
What if we just swap desks every month so it's fair to both of us?
Let's ask the manager to decide, since neither of us seems to be able to agree on it.
quests.hint: Look for an arrangement that works for both.
quests.explanation: A rotating arrangement solves the problem fairly. Claiming seniority, giving in, or escalating don't create a shared solution.
quests.culturalNote: Rotation is a common fair-share tactic in shared workspaces.

quests.scene: You and your brother both want your late mother's watch, and emotions are running high.
options: I was the one who looked after her at the end, so I think I should get the watch.
You can have the watch, I don't want to fight about it, and it's not that important.
Mum's watch means a lot to both of us. Could we each list what matters most, and see where we overlap?
Let's ask a lawyer to divide everything fairly, since we obviously can't agree on our own.
quests.hint: Find out what matters to each side.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging shared meaning and comparing priorities opens the way to a fair outcome. Claiming merit, giving in, or lawyering-up close the conversation.
quests.culturalNote: Inheritance disputes are often emotional rather than financial, so listening first helps.

quests.scene: You're frustrated with a teammate's habits but want to raise it with your manager without attacking her.
options: I'd like to raise something about the team workflow. Can we find a time to talk?
Priya has been making my life impossible, and I need you to do something about her immediately.
I don't want to get anyone in trouble, but there are a few issues that some people on the team have been having lately.
I've collected a list of Priya's mistakes, and I'd like to go through them with you tomorrow.
quests.hint: Raise the issue neutrally and ask for a conversation.
quests.explanation: Framing it around workflow and asking for a time keeps it professional. Personal attacks, vague hints, or lists of faults invite defensiveness.
quests.culturalNote: Managers usually prefer specific work issues over personal complaints.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to escalate.
quests.scene: A support agent has been unable to help after twenty minutes and you'd like to move the issue up.
options: You clearly can't help me with this, so I want someone who actually knows what they're doing to take this call.
Could I speak to a supervisor about this, please, since we haven't made much progress?
I've explained this three times already, so I'm going to have to ask you to escalate it right now.
Perhaps someone else might be able to look at this, if you don't mind me asking, sorry to bother you.
quests.hint: Ask directly without insulting the agent.
quests.explanation: A polite direct request to escalate is clear and respectful. Insults, demands, or excessive hedging make it harder.
quests.culturalNote: Asking for a supervisor is normal and usually acceptable.

quests.scene: A teammate submitted the group project without telling anyone.
options: You submitted without asking us, which was really selfish, and now we could all get a bad grade.
It's fine that you submitted it, but it's a bit annoying that nobody told the rest of us.
I'll tell the teacher that I had nothing to do with this submission, so I don't lose marks.
I saw the project was submitted. I'd have liked to review it first. Can we agree to confirm before submitting next time?
quests.hint: Name the impact and propose a process.
quests.explanation: Stating your concern and proposing a rule for the future is fair and forward-looking. Blame, passive complaint, or distancing yourself don't fix the process.
quests.culturalNote: Setting a team rule after a mishap is a common way to prevent repeat issues.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to reconnect.
quests.scene: You and a close friend haven't spoken since an argument two weeks ago. You want to repair things.
options: I miss talking to you a lot lately. Can we grab coffee sometime this week?
I'm still upset about what happened, but I suppose we should probably talk about it at some point.
I've been thinking about our argument, and I think you owe me an apology before we speak again.
Hey, it's been a while! How have you been? Let's forget about the whole thing, shall we?
quests.hint: Reach out with warmth and a concrete invitation.
quests.explanation: A simple, warm invitation lowers the stakes. Lingering resentment, demands, or pretending nothing happened aren't good starting points.
quests.culturalNote: Reaching out first is often appreciated after a fight, even if you weren't the one at fault.

quests.scene: Your neighbor put up a fence that seems to be on your side of the line.
options: The fence is on my property line, so I don't think there's anything to discuss about it.
I'm fine with whatever you want to do about the fence, as long as it doesn't cost me anything.
I'll ask the council to check the boundary, and then we can both see who's right about it.
I'd like to understand what you're hoping for with the fence. Could we look at it together this weekend?
quests.hint: Start by understanding and propose a joint look.
quests.explanation: Asking about their goal and inviting a joint look keeps the neighbor relationship intact. Claiming ownership or going straight to the council escalates.
quests.culturalNote: Boundary disputes are best resolved early and with evidence.

quests.instruction: Pick the best way to mediate.
quests.scene: Two of your team members clash constantly and you've been asked to help.
options: You two need to sort this out yourselves, because it's affecting the whole team and it's unprofessional.
I'd like to hear from each of you separately first, and then we can find a time to talk together.
Let's all sit down together right now and say everything that's been bothering us, openly and.
I'll talk to your manager about moving one of you to another team, since you clearly can't get along.
quests.hint: Listen to each side before bringing them together.
quests.explanation: Speaking to each person separately lets you understand before a joint conversation. Ordering, forcing a confrontation, or reassigning skips the listening.
quests.culturalNote: Separate conversations often reveal issues people won't say in front of each other.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to set a limit.
quests.scene: A coworker jokes about your accent in front of others. You find it hurtful.
options: I'd rather you didn't joke about my accent. I'd appreciate it if you'd stop.
That was a really offensive thing to say, and I think you should be ashamed of yourself for it.
It's okay, I've heard it before, so you don't need to worry about it.
Ha, very funny. Maybe I should start joking about your accent as well, to see how you like it.
quests.hint: State your limit plainly and calmly.
quests.explanation: A calm, direct request is hard to dispute and sets a clear limit. Shaming, brushing off, or retaliating don't stop the behavior.
quests.culturalNote: Workplace conduct policies often cover comments about accent or origin; check yours if it continues.

quests.scene: You overhear a rumor about you circulating at work and want to find out where it started.
options: Someone has been spreading rumors about me, and I want to find out who is responsible immediately.
I'm sure it's nothing, but I heard something odd, and I wanted to check that it isn't true.
I don't care what people say about me, so I won't be doing anything about it.
I heard something about me. I'd like to know where it started.
quests.hint: Be direct without accusing anyone yet.
quests.explanation: A direct request for the source gets facts without accusing. Vague concern, blame, or dismissal don't help.
quests.culturalNote: Rumors are best tackled by asking calmly rather than hunting for culprits.

quests.scene: You've noticed your workload is far heavier than a colleague's, and you'd like to raise it with your manager.
options: It's not fair that I have twice as many accounts as Jamie, and I think you're favoring him over me.
I've noticed I'm handling more accounts than the rest of the team. Could we review how work is being shared?
I don't mind taking extra accounts, but I'd appreciate some recognition or maybe a bonus for it.
I'm managing, so there's really no need to change anything, but I thought I would mention it.
quests.hint: Present facts and ask for a review.
quests.explanation: Sticking to facts and asking for a review invites a fair discussion. Accusing favoritism or downplaying the issue doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Comparing workloads is easier when framed around fairness of process.

quests.scene: A shop has refused your refund request because of its policy. The item was faulty.
options: Your policy is ridiculous, and I'll tell everyone I know to avoid this shop if you don't refund me.
I understand the policy. Could I speak to the manager about an exception, given the item was faulty?
I suppose there's nothing more I can do, so I'll keep it and try to get it repaired myself.
I'm not leaving until I get my money back, and I'll wait here as long as it takes.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the rule and ask for a route around it.
quests.explanation: Recognizing the policy and asking about an exception is firm without hostility. Threats, giving up, or standing your ground rarely help.
quests.culturalNote: Consumer law may protect you when goods are faulty, and it varies by country.

quests.scene: Your flight is overbooked and the gate agent says you may not get a seat.
options: You've overbooked the flight, which is unacceptable, and I demand to be put on the next one.
I don't mind giving up my seat if it helps, and I'm sure you'll do what's best for everyone.
What compensation and alternatives can you offer me?
I have an important meeting, so please find a way to get me on the plane, whatever it takes.
quests.hint: Ask about options instead of demanding.
quests.explanation: Asking about compensation and alternatives is practical and calm. Demands, volunteering, or pleading are less effective.
quests.culturalNote: Overbooking compensation rules vary between airlines and countries.

quests.scene: A friend cancels a trip at the last minute after you both paid a non-refundable deposit.
options: You've wasted my money by cancelling, and I think you owe me everything I put down for the trip.
I understand things came up. I've paid a non-refundable deposit, so could we talk about how to share that cost?
It's fine, I'll cover the deposit myself, and we can go on another trip when you're ready.
I'm disappointed, but I guess these things happen, so let's not talk about the deposit right now.
quests.hint: Acknowledge her situation and raise the money question fairly.
quests.explanation: Being understanding while raising the cost keeps the friendship and the fairness. Blame, silent absorption, or avoidance don't.
quests.culturalNote: Money conflicts between friends are easier when raised early and calmly.

quests.scene: A shop beneath your flat plays loud music after ten, which affects your sleep.
options: The noise after ten is affecting my sleep. Could we agree on quieter hours, or could you tell me who to talk to?
Your shop's noise is unbearable, and if it continues, I'll have to complain to the council.
I don't want to cause any trouble, but sometimes the music is a bit loud in the evenings, that's all.
I know you have a business to run, so I'll just wear earplugs and try to get used to it.
quests.hint: Describe the effect and propose a limit.
quests.explanation: Naming the time, the effect, and a possible agreement is polite and specific. Threats, vague hints, or giving in don't solve it.
quests.culturalNote: Noise rules and hours vary by location, so local regulations can help if talk fails.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to raise this.
quests.scene: Your coach keeps benching you and you'd like more playing time.
options: It's unfair that you never let me play, and I think you have favorites on the team.
Could we talk about what I can work on to get more playing time?
I understand your decision, and I'll keep training as hard as I can, even if I don't play.
I'm thinking about quitting the team if I'm not going to get a fair chance soon.
quests.hint: Ask what to improve instead of demanding time.
quests.explanation: A growth-focused question invites concrete feedback. Accusations, silent acceptance, or threats don't help you play.
quests.culturalNote: Coaches usually respond to players who ask how to improve.

quests.scene: Someone cuts in line at the ticket counter in front of you and others.
options: Hey, no cutting in! Everyone here has been waiting for a long time, so go to the back.
I think you might have missed the end of the line, but it's probably no big deal, really.
Excuse me, the line starts back there — we've all been waiting.
Some people have no manners at all, do they? Some of us have been here for an hour.
quests.hint: Be clear and civil.
quests.explanation: A polite, clear pointer to the line is hard to argue with. Shouting, excusing, or sarcasm each cause problems.
quests.culturalNote: Queueing norms are strong in some places; a calm reminder is usually enough.
